metadata.title: Cardiovascular Nutrition Mastery Bank
metadata.targetAudience: Dietitians and clinical nutrition professionals aiming for advanced/senior mastery
metadata.purpose: Evidence-grounded multiple-choice mastery bank spanning nutrient targets, food selection, label reading, calculations, guideline interpretation and clinical decision-making.
metadata.masteryPrinciple: Questions intentionally test application and context, not only recall. Disease-specific targets are labeled by guideline context to avoid false universal rules.

recommendedAppLogic.initialPass: Randomize within domains and require >=80% overall before advancing.
recommendedAppLogic.masteryThreshold: >=90% in every domain with no critical-safety misses in the latest 20 questions.
recommendedAppLogic.spacedRepetition: Repeat missed questions after 1 day, 3 days, 7 days and 21 days; then use variant questions.
recommendedAppLogic.adaptiveRule: Increase clinical_reasoning and calculation items when recall accuracy exceeds 85%.
criticalSafetyTopics: fluid restriction is not universal in heart failure
diet does not replace guideline-directed medication after MI/ASCVD

metadata.disclaimer: Educational content for professional learning. Patient-specific recommendations require individualized assessment, local protocols and the treating clinical team's orders.

include: saturated fat percentages and gram conversions
acute postoperative nutrition vs intentional weight loss

questions.question: Which swap best lowers saturated fat while preserving an unsaturated-fat source?

options.text: Replace butter with olive or canola oil.
Replace olive oil with coconut oil.

questions.correctAnswer: Replace butter with olive or canola oil.
questions.explanation: Liquid non-tropical plant oils are rich in unsaturated fats and are preferred in place of saturated-fat sources such as butter, ghee, coconut and palm oils.
questions.clinicalPearl: The benefit is primarily from replacement: what replaces saturated fat matters.

questions.question: What is the main lipid effect of excess saturated fat that concerns a cardiovascular dietitian?

options.text: It tends to raise LDL cholesterol.
It selectively lowers triglycerides without affecting LDL.

questions.correctAnswer: It tends to raise LDL cholesterol.
questions.explanation: Saturated fat can increase LDL-C; replacing it with unsaturated fat is a central dietary strategy for reducing atherogenic lipid exposure.
questions.clinicalPearl: Do not teach 'low fat' in isolation; teach fat quality.

questions.question: Which statement best reflects the 2026 AHA dietary guidance for the general population?

options.text: Dietary saturated fat is no longer relevant if total calories are controlled.
Everyone with or without CVD must consume exactly 6% of calories from saturated fat.
Coconut oil is preferred because it is plant-based.
Heart-healthy dietary patterns are typically unlikely to exceed 10% of energy from saturated fat, with emphasis on replacing saturated fat with unsaturated fat.

questions.correctAnswer: Heart-healthy dietary patterns are typically unlikely to exceed 10% of energy from saturated fat, with emphasis on replacing saturated fat with unsaturated fat.
questions.explanation: The 2026 AHA statement emphasizes dietary patterns and substitution with unsaturated fat; it notes heart-healthy patterns are generally unlikely to exceed 10% of energy from saturated fat.
questions.clinicalPearl: General-population guidance and disease-specific therapeutic targets are not always identical.

questions.question: A patient with established coronary disease is prescribed a 2,000-kcal diet with saturated fat limited to 6% of energy. Approximately how many grams of saturated fat is that per day?
questions.explanation: 6% of 2,000 kcal = 120 kcal. Fat provides 9 kcal/g, so 120 ÷ 9 ≈ 13.3 g.
questions.clinicalPearl: Be able to convert a percentage-of-energy fat target into grams at bedside speed.

questions.question: On a 1,800-kcal diet, 10% of energy from saturated fat equals approximately how many grams?
questions.clinicalPearl: Fat calories are converted to grams by dividing by 9.

questions.question: Which food is most likely to be relatively high in saturated fat?
questions.correctAnswer: Butter
questions.explanation: Butter is a major saturated-fat source. Olive oil, walnuts and flaxseed are predominantly sources of unsaturated fats.
questions.clinicalPearl: Plant origin does not automatically mean low saturated fat; coconut and palm oils are key exceptions.

questions.question: Which plant fat is an important exception to the rule that plant oils are usually rich in unsaturated fat?
questions.correctAnswer: Coconut oil
questions.explanation: Coconut and palm oils are tropical oils and are relatively high in saturated fat.
questions.clinicalPearl: Teach 'non-tropical liquid plant oils' rather than simply 'vegetable oils'.

questions.question: Which ingredient-list term most strongly signals a source of industrial trans fat?
questions.correctAnswer: Partially hydrogenated oil
questions.explanation: Partially hydrogenated oils are a classic source of industrial trans fat.
questions.clinicalPearl: A label can show 0 g trans fat per serving while still listing partially hydrogenated oil if the amount is below the labeling threshold.

questions.question: A food label states '0 g trans fat' but the ingredients include partially hydrogenated oil. What is the best interpretation?

options.text: The product contains only saturated fat, not trans fat.
The ingredient list is irrelevant because 0 g always means none is present.
The product may still contain a small amount of trans fat per serving.

questions.correctAnswer: The product may still contain a small amount of trans fat per serving.
questions.explanation: Small amounts may round to 0 g on the label; the ingredient list provides additional information.
questions.clinicalPearl: Always teach dietitians to read both Nutrition Facts and the ingredient list.

questions.question: What combination of lipoprotein effects is classically associated with industrial trans fat?

options.text: Higher HDL with no LDL effect
Lower LDL and lower triglycerides only

questions.correctAnswer: Higher LDL and lower HDL
questions.explanation: Trans fat adversely affects lipoproteins, including raising LDL and lowering HDL.
questions.clinicalPearl: Avoid industrial trans fat rather than trying to fit it into a discretionary allowance.

questions.question: Which food is a classic source of monounsaturated fat?

options.text: Shortening made with partially hydrogenated oil

questions.correctAnswer: Olive oil
questions.explanation: Olive oil is rich in monounsaturated fatty acids and is a core fat source in Mediterranean-style eating.
questions.clinicalPearl: MUFA-rich foods are useful when they replace saturated-fat sources.

questions.question: Which food is a good source of polyunsaturated fat?
questions.correctAnswer: Walnuts
questions.explanation: Walnuts contain substantial polyunsaturated fat, including alpha-linolenic acid.
questions.clinicalPearl: Nuts add unsaturated fat, fiber and plant protein but remain energy-dense.

questions.question: A patient asks whether all fat should be minimized to lower cardiovascular risk. What is the best response?

options.text: Increase coconut oil because it raises HDL.
Ignore fat quality if body weight is normal.
Focus on replacing saturated and trans fats with unsaturated fats rather than minimizing all fat.
Eliminate nearly all fat, including nuts and olive oil.

questions.correctAnswer: Focus on replacing saturated and trans fats with unsaturated fats rather than minimizing all fat.
questions.explanation: Current cardiovascular guidance emphasizes fat quality and replacement, not indiscriminate fat restriction.
questions.clinicalPearl: The question is not merely 'how much fat?' but 'which fat, replacing what?'.

questions.question: Which replacement is most consistent with lowering LDL-C?

options.text: Replace butter with a polyunsaturated-rich liquid plant oil.
Replace olive oil with coconut oil.

questions.correctAnswer: Replace butter with a polyunsaturated-rich liquid plant oil.
questions.explanation: Replacing saturated fat with unsaturated fat, particularly PUFA, lowers LDL-C more effectively than replacing saturated fat with refined carbohydrate.
questions.clinicalPearl: Replacement nutrient determines much of the cardiometabolic effect.

questions.question: Which cooking-fat recommendation is most aligned with AHA guidance?

options.text: Use ghee as the default because it is minimally processed.
Prefer coconut oil over all seed oils.
Use non-tropical liquid plant oils such as olive, canola, corn, soybean or sunflower oil.
Use shortening containing partially hydrogenated oils for high-heat cooking.

questions.correctAnswer: Use non-tropical liquid plant oils such as olive, canola, corn, soybean or sunflower oil.
questions.explanation: Non-tropical liquid plant oils provide unsaturated fats and are preferred over solid fats and tropical oils.
questions.clinicalPearl: Avoid false dichotomies such as 'natural fat good, seed oil bad'; evaluate fatty-acid profile and overall pattern.

questions.question: Why can two credible cardiovascular guidelines appear to give different saturated-fat percentages?

options.text: Saturated fat has no measurable effect on LDL.
Percent-of-energy targets are identical across all populations.
One guideline must therefore be fraudulent.
Targets may differ by population and clinical context, such as general prevention versus established coronary disease.

questions.correctAnswer: Targets may differ by population and clinical context, such as general prevention versus established coronary disease.
questions.explanation: Guideline targets are population-specific. Therapeutic secondary-prevention guidance may be stricter than broad population dietary guidance.
questions.clinicalPearl: Teach the source, year and patient population together with the number.

questions.question: Which meal best demonstrates a saturated-to-unsaturated fat substitution?

options.text: Fried chicken with buttered white bread.
Pastry made with shortening and cream.
Grilled fish, vegetables and whole grains dressed with olive oil instead of a butter-based sauce.

questions.correctAnswer: Grilled fish, vegetables and whole grains dressed with olive oil instead of a butter-based sauce.
questions.explanation: The first meal replaces solid saturated-fat sources with fish and olive oil while adding minimally processed plant foods.
questions.clinicalPearl: Evaluate the whole plate, not a single nutrient in isolation.

questions.question: Why can excessive portions of even heart-healthy oils interfere with weight reduction?

options.text: Plant oils provide only 2 kcal per gram.
All fats provide about 9 kcal per gram.

questions.correctAnswer: All fats provide about 9 kcal per gram.
questions.explanation: MUFA and PUFA are cardiometabolically preferable to saturated fat, but all fat remains energy-dense at about 9 kcal/g.
questions.clinicalPearl: Quality and quantity both matter when weight loss is a goal.

questions.question: A patient has LDL-C above goal and uses large amounts of ghee because it is 'traditional and natural.' What is the most appropriate dietetic approach?

options.text: Recommend replacing ghee with coconut oil.
Tell the patient all traditional foods are unhealthy.
Respect the food culture, quantify intake, and negotiate partial replacement with unsaturated oils while improving the overall dietary pattern.
Focus only on dietary cholesterol and ignore ghee.

questions.correctAnswer: Respect the food culture, quantify intake, and negotiate partial replacement with unsaturated oils while improving the overall dietary pattern.
questions.explanation: Effective counseling combines evidence-based fat substitution with culturally acceptable, sustainable changes.
questions.clinicalPearl: Clinical excellence includes adherence engineering, not just nutrient knowledge.

questions.question: Which advice is strongest regarding industrial trans fat?

options.text: Target exactly 10% of calories from trans fat.
Use trans fat instead of PUFA to improve HDL.
Avoid it as much as practicable and check for partially hydrogenated oils.
Trans fat is acceptable if sodium is low.

questions.correctAnswer: Avoid it as much as practicable and check for partially hydrogenated oils.
questions.explanation: Industrial trans fat has an adverse cardiovascular profile and should be avoided rather than treated as a routine calorie allowance.
questions.clinicalPearl: A low-sodium food is not automatically cardioprotective if its fat quality is poor.

questions.question: How often does the AHA recommend eating fish, particularly fatty fish, as part of a heart-healthy pattern?
questions.correctAnswer: About 2 servings per week
questions.explanation: The AHA recommends two servings of fish per week, especially fatty fish.
questions.clinicalPearl: Food-first omega-3 advice differs from prescribing concentrated omega-3 medication.

questions.question: Approximately how much cooked fish counts as one AHA serving?
questions.correctAnswer: 3 oz cooked (about 85 g)
questions.explanation: A standard serving is about 3 ounces cooked, roughly 85 grams.
questions.clinicalPearl: Know both ounce and gram equivalents for international practice.

questions.question: Which fish is especially rich in EPA and DHA?
questions.correctAnswer: Salmon
questions.explanation: Fatty fish such as salmon, sardines, mackerel and herring are rich in long-chain omega-3 fatty acids.
questions.clinicalPearl: Not all fish contain the same amount of EPA/DHA.

questions.question: Which food is a meaningful plant source of alpha-linolenic acid (ALA)?
questions.correctAnswer: Ground flaxseed
questions.explanation: Flaxseed, chia, walnuts and some plant oils supply ALA.
questions.clinicalPearl: ALA is an essential omega-3 fatty acid; conversion to EPA/DHA is limited.

questions.question: Which statement about ALA is most accurate?

options.text: ALA is converted to EPA and DHA with 100% efficiency.
ALA is found only in fish.
ALA is a saturated fatty acid.
The body can convert some ALA to EPA and DHA, but conversion is limited.

questions.correctAnswer: The body can convert some ALA to EPA and DHA, but conversion is limited.
questions.explanation: Plant ALA contributes to omega-3 intake, but endogenous conversion to EPA and DHA is limited.
questions.clinicalPearl: Do not present flaxseed and salmon as nutritionally identical omega-3 sources.

questions.question: A patient with coronary disease asks whether over-the-counter fish-oil capsules can replace evidence-based lipid-lowering therapy. What is the best answer?

options.text: No. Supplements should not replace guideline-directed lipid-lowering therapy; indication-specific prescription therapies are a separate issue.
Yes, if the capsule contains at least 100 mg of omega-3.
Yes, any fish-oil supplement is equivalent to a statin.
Yes, provided dietary sodium is low.

questions.correctAnswer: No. Supplements should not replace guideline-directed lipid-lowering therapy; indication-specific prescription therapies are a separate issue.
questions.explanation: Dietary supplements are not recommended as substitutes for proven lipid-lowering therapy. Prescription omega-3 products may have specific indications under medical management.
questions.clinicalPearl: Separate food advice, supplements and prescription pharmacotherapy.

questions.question: Which meal best increases omega-3 intake without adding substantial saturated fat?

options.text: Baked salmon with vegetables and barley

questions.correctAnswer: Baked salmon with vegetables and barley
questions.explanation: Fatty fish plus vegetables and whole grains fits a heart-healthy pattern and supplies EPA/DHA.
questions.clinicalPearl: Preparation method can undermine an otherwise healthy protein choice.

questions.question: For severe hypertriglyceridemia, which statement is most accurate?

options.text: Lifestyle and statin-based ASCVD risk management remain foundational; selected patients may need triglyceride-lowering pharmacotherapy under medical care.
All omega-3 supplements have identical dose and evidence.
Triglycerides are unrelated to pancreatitis risk.
Eating two fish servings weekly is always sufficient treatment.

questions.correctAnswer: Lifestyle and statin-based ASCVD risk management remain foundational; selected patients may need triglyceride-lowering pharmacotherapy under medical care.
questions.explanation: The 2026 dyslipidemia guideline keeps lifestyle and statins central, with additional therapy for selected patients, especially when triglycerides are very high.
questions.clinicalPearl: Do not confuse dietary fish recommendations with therapeutic-dose prescription omega-3.

questions.question: Which type of fiber is particularly useful for lowering LDL-C?
questions.correctAnswer: Soluble/viscous fiber
questions.explanation: Soluble/viscous fibers can reduce intestinal cholesterol/bile-acid reabsorption and help lower LDL-C.
questions.clinicalPearl: Oats, barley, legumes and psyllium are practical soluble-fiber sources.

questions.question: Which breakfast is most likely to provide substantial soluble fiber?

options.text: Oatmeal topped with berries and nuts

questions.correctAnswer: Oatmeal topped with berries and nuts
questions.explanation: Oats contain beta-glucan, a viscous soluble fiber, and fruit adds additional fiber.
questions.clinicalPearl: Build fiber through intact foods, not isolated supplements alone.

questions.question: What is the best way to verify that a brown-colored bread is actually whole grain?

options.text: Assume brown color means whole grain.
Check that a whole grain is listed prominently in the ingredient list.
Choose the product with the most sodium.

questions.correctAnswer: Check that a whole grain is listed prominently in the ingredient list.
questions.explanation: Color can come from molasses or coloring; ingredient lists provide better evidence of whole-grain content.
questions.clinicalPearl: Front-of-pack marketing is not a substitute for ingredient-list literacy.

questions.question: According to AHA consumer label guidance, roughly what fiber intake range do many adults need for good health?
questions.correctAnswer: About 25–34 g/day
questions.explanation: AHA label guidance notes that adults generally need at least about 25–34 grams of fiber daily.
questions.clinicalPearl: Individual requirements vary with age, sex, energy intake and clinical context.

questions.question: How can high-fiber foods support weight reduction?

options.text: They often increase satiety and lower dietary energy density.
Fiber automatically blocks all fat absorption.
They eliminate the need for calorie balance.

questions.correctAnswer: They often increase satiety and lower dietary energy density.
questions.explanation: Fiber-rich foods can improve fullness and often displace more energy-dense foods.
questions.clinicalPearl: Fiber helps, but weight loss still depends on sustained energy balance.

questions.question: A patient increases fiber from 10 g/day to 35 g/day overnight and develops bloating. What is the best advice?

options.text: Increase fiber more gradually and ensure appropriate fluid intake unless fluid is restricted.

questions.correctAnswer: Increase fiber more gradually and ensure appropriate fluid intake unless fluid is restricted.
questions.explanation: Rapid increases in fiber may cause GI symptoms. Gradual titration and adequate fluid are often better tolerated, while respecting any prescribed fluid restriction.
questions.clinicalPearl: Fiber counseling must consider GI tolerance and comorbid heart failure.

questions.question: Why are legumes useful in cardiovascular nutrition?

options.text: They are always high in sodium even when cooked without salt.
They are naturally rich in trans fat.
They provide fiber and plant protein with little saturated fat.

questions.correctAnswer: They provide fiber and plant protein with little saturated fat.
questions.explanation: Beans, lentils and peas combine fiber, minerals and plant protein and can replace higher-saturated-fat protein sources.
questions.clinicalPearl: Canned legumes can be rinsed and lower-sodium versions chosen.

questions.question: On a Nutrition Facts label, which % Daily Value convention generally indicates a nutrient is high per serving?
questions.correctAnswer: 20% DV or more
questions.explanation: A common label rule of thumb is 5% DV or less is low and 20% DV or more is high.
questions.clinicalPearl: Use %DV to compare similar products quickly, especially fiber, sodium and saturated fat.

questions.question: What is the AHA upper sodium limit commonly recommended for most adults?
questions.correctAnswer: No more than 2,300 mg/day
questions.explanation: AHA guidance recommends no more than 2,300 mg sodium daily, with an ideal goal of about 1,500 mg for many adults, especially for blood-pressure lowering.
questions.clinicalPearl: Always distinguish sodium from salt.

questions.question: What sodium target can lower blood pressure further within the DASH framework?
questions.correctAnswer: 1,500 mg/day
questions.explanation: NHLBI DASH materials note that 1,500 mg/day can lower blood pressure further than 2,300 mg/day.
questions.clinicalPearl: A stricter sodium target should still be individualized for clinical status and adherence.

questions.question: WHO's limit of less than 2 g sodium per day is approximately equivalent to how much salt (sodium chloride)?
questions.correctAnswer: Less than 5 g salt/day
questions.explanation: Sodium is about 39–40% of sodium chloride by weight, so 2 g sodium is approximately 5 g salt.
questions.clinicalPearl: Patients often confuse 'sodium' and 'salt'; dietitians should be fluent in both units.

questions.question: Where does most dietary sodium commonly come from in modern food environments?

options.text: The sodium naturally present in drinking water alone

questions.correctAnswer: Packaged, prepared and restaurant foods
questions.explanation: A large share of sodium comes from processed, prepared and restaurant foods rather than only from the salt shaker.
questions.clinicalPearl: Sodium counseling must include labels, condiments, breads, sauces and restaurant meals.

questions.question: A soup contains 680 mg sodium per serving and the patient eats 2 servings. How much sodium did they consume?
questions.explanation: 680 × 2 = 1,360 mg sodium.
questions.clinicalPearl: Serving-size math is one of the highest-yield practical skills in sodium counseling.

questions.question: Two breads are nutritionally similar except Bread A has 80 mg sodium/slice and Bread B has 190 mg/slice. For a patient reducing sodium, which is preferable?
questions.correctAnswer: Bread A
questions.explanation: When other factors are comparable, the lower-sodium product helps reduce cumulative daily sodium.
questions.clinicalPearl: Frequently eaten foods can make large contributions even when they do not taste very salty.

questions.question: DASH stands for:

options.text: Dietary Allocation for Sodium and Hydration

questions.correctAnswer: Dietary Approaches to Stop Hypertension
questions.explanation: DASH is the Dietary Approaches to Stop Hypertension eating pattern.
questions.clinicalPearl: Know the acronym, but more importantly know the actual food pattern.

questions.question: Which pattern best describes DASH?

options.text: High in processed meat, refined grains and salty snacks.
High in vegetables, fruits, whole grains, legumes/nuts and low-fat dairy, with lower sodium and saturated fat.

questions.correctAnswer: High in vegetables, fruits, whole grains, legumes/nuts and low-fat dairy, with lower sodium and saturated fat.
questions.explanation: DASH emphasizes plant foods, low-fat dairy, lean proteins and lower sodium/saturated fat.
questions.clinicalPearl: DASH is a food pattern, not merely a sodium restriction.

questions.question: In a 2,000-kcal DASH pattern, approximately how many vegetable servings are recommended per day?
questions.correctAnswer: 4–5 servings
questions.explanation: The standard 2,000-kcal DASH example includes about 4–5 vegetable servings daily.
questions.clinicalPearl: Serving targets change with calorie needs; know the reference pattern and how to adapt it.

questions.question: In a 2,000-kcal DASH pattern, approximately how many fruit servings are recommended per day?
questions.correctAnswer: 4–5 servings
questions.explanation: The standard 2,000-kcal DASH example includes about 4–5 fruit servings daily.
questions.clinicalPearl: Whole fruit is generally preferred over sweetened fruit products.

questions.question: In a 2,000-kcal DASH pattern, low-fat or fat-free dairy is typically:
questions.correctAnswer: 2–3 servings/day
questions.explanation: NHLBI's 2,000-kcal DASH example includes 2–3 daily servings of low-fat or fat-free dairy.
questions.clinicalPearl: Adapt for lactose intolerance, allergy, vegan preference and overall nutrient adequacy.

questions.question: In a 2,000-kcal DASH pattern, nuts, seeds and dry beans/peas are typically recommended:
questions.correctAnswer: About 4–5 servings per week
questions.explanation: The standard DASH pattern uses several servings of nuts, seeds and legumes each week.
questions.clinicalPearl: Weekly food-group targets are easy to forget and worth drilling in a mastery app.

questions.question: How can higher dietary potassium help blood pressure in appropriate patients?

options.text: It raises blood pressure by constricting vessels.
It has no relationship to sodium handling.
It can blunt sodium's effects and promote sodium excretion while supporting vascular relaxation.

questions.correctAnswer: It can blunt sodium's effects and promote sodium excretion while supporting vascular relaxation.
questions.explanation: Potassium-rich diets can support blood-pressure reduction through renal sodium handling and vascular effects.
questions.clinicalPearl: Food-based potassium is valuable, but safety depends on kidney function and medications.

questions.question: Which patient needs the most caution before intentionally increasing potassium or using a potassium-based salt substitute?

options.text: A patient with chronic kidney disease taking a potassium-raising medication
A patient eating too few vegetables
A healthy runner with normal labs
A healthy adult with normal kidney function

questions.correctAnswer: A patient with chronic kidney disease taking a potassium-raising medication
questions.explanation: Kidney disease and medications such as RAAS inhibitors or potassium-sparing agents can increase hyperkalemia risk.
questions.clinicalPearl: Never give blanket 'eat more potassium' advice without screening for contraindications.

questions.question: For otherwise appropriate adults with elevated or high blood pressure, AHA educational guidance commonly cites what dietary potassium range?
questions.correctAnswer: About 3,500–5,000 mg/day, ideally from foods
questions.explanation: AHA hypertension materials cite roughly 3,500–5,000 mg/day from dietary sources for appropriate adults, with clinical caution where potassium handling is impaired.
questions.clinicalPearl: This is not a universal prescription for CKD, hyperkalemia or potassium-raising medications.

questions.question: Under the 2025 AHA/ACC framework, which blood pressure is classified as stage 1 hypertension?
questions.correctAnswer: 132/84 mm Hg
questions.explanation: Stage 1 hypertension is systolic 130–139 mm Hg or diastolic 80–89 mm Hg.
questions.clinicalPearl: Dietitians should recognize BP categories because nutrition counseling intensity depends on risk and treatment context.

questions.question: Under the 2025 AHA/ACC framework, stage 2 hypertension begins at:
questions.correctAnswer: ≥140 systolic or ≥90 diastolic mm Hg
questions.explanation: Stage 2 hypertension is defined as systolic ≥140 or diastolic ≥90 mm Hg.
questions.clinicalPearl: Use the higher category when systolic and diastolic fall into different categories.

questions.question: Which package of lifestyle changes is most consistent with current hypertension guidance?

options.text: DASH-style eating, sodium reduction, adequate dietary potassium when safe, healthy weight, physical activity and less/no alcohol.

questions.correctAnswer: DASH-style eating, sodium reduction, adequate dietary potassium when safe, healthy weight, physical activity and less/no alcohol.
questions.explanation: Hypertension nutrition is multimodal; sodium reduction is important but not the sole intervention.
questions.clinicalPearl: A mastery quiz should test combined intervention planning, not isolated facts.

questions.question: For many adults, reducing sodium intake by approximately how much per day can improve blood pressure even if the ideal target is not reached?

options.text: No reduction is useful unless sodium reaches zero

questions.correctAnswer: About 1,000 mg/day
questions.explanation: A reduction of around 1,000 mg/day can improve BP and may be more achievable than an immediate jump to an ideal target.
questions.clinicalPearl: Use stepped goals when adherence is the barrier.

questions.question: A hypertensive patient wants to use potassium chloride salt substitute. What should the dietitian check first?

options.text: Kidney function, serum potassium and medications affecting potassium balance

questions.correctAnswer: Kidney function, serum potassium and medications affecting potassium balance
questions.explanation: Potassium-containing salt substitutes can be useful for some adults but may be unsafe in patients at risk of hyperkalemia.
questions.clinicalPearl: A 'lower sodium' product can still require clinical screening.

questions.question: Which strategy is most useful for reducing sodium when eating out?

options.text: Request sauces/dressings on the side, choose minimally processed dishes, and avoid heavily cured or salted items.
Assume restaurant food is low-sodium unless it tastes salty.
Choose soup and processed meat at every meal.

questions.correctAnswer: Request sauces/dressings on the side, choose minimally processed dishes, and avoid heavily cured or salted items.
questions.explanation: Restaurant sauces, soups, cured foods and prepared dishes can contain large sodium loads.
questions.clinicalPearl: Taste is an unreliable measure of sodium content.

questions.question: The AHA recommends keeping added sugars to approximately what share of calories or less?

options.text: There is no reason to limit added sugar

questions.correctAnswer: About 6% of calories
questions.explanation: AHA consumer guidance recommends limiting added sugars to about 6% of daily calories.
questions.clinicalPearl: Distinguish added sugars from naturally occurring sugars in intact fruit and plain milk.

questions.question: What is the AHA's commonly cited daily added-sugar limit for most women?
questions.correctAnswer: About 25 g (6 teaspoons)
questions.explanation: AHA guidance commonly cites no more than about 25 g or 6 teaspoons of added sugar daily for women.
questions.clinicalPearl: Use gram-to-teaspoon conversion during label counseling: roughly 4 g sugar per teaspoon.

questions.question: What is the AHA's commonly cited daily added-sugar limit for most men?
questions.correctAnswer: About 36 g (9 teaspoons)
questions.explanation: AHA guidance commonly cites no more than about 36 g or 9 teaspoons of added sugar daily for men.
questions.clinicalPearl: These are practical public-facing limits; individualized energy needs still matter.

questions.question: A drink contains 32 g added sugar. Approximately how many teaspoons of added sugar is that?
questions.correctAnswer: 8 teaspoons
questions.explanation: One teaspoon of sugar is approximately 4 g; 32 ÷ 4 = 8 teaspoons.
questions.clinicalPearl: Converting grams to teaspoons can make counseling more tangible.

questions.question: Which is usually the better cardiovascular choice?
questions.correctAnswer: Whole fruit
questions.explanation: Whole fruit provides fiber and micronutrients without the concentrated added sugar load of sweetened beverages.
questions.clinicalPearl: Do not conflate whole fruit with sugar-sweetened fruit-flavored drinks.

questions.question: What is the best current interpretation of dietary cholesterol in cardiovascular prevention?

options.text: Only dietary cholesterol matters; saturated fat is irrelevant.
Dietary cholesterol has no biological effect in any person.
For most people it is not the primary dietary target; overall dietary pattern and saturated-fat replacement are more important.
Everyone must stay below exactly 100 mg/day.

questions.correctAnswer: For most people it is not the primary dietary target; overall dietary pattern and saturated-fat replacement are more important.
questions.explanation: The 2026 AHA dietary statement notes that dietary cholesterol is no longer a primary target for most people within an overall heart-healthy pattern.
questions.clinicalPearl: Do not turn 'not primary target' into 'unlimited intake'.

questions.question: Which counseling approach is most evidence-aligned for eggs?

options.text: Focus only on egg color and size.
Consider eggs within the whole dietary pattern, especially the patient's LDL-C, saturated-fat intake and foods eaten with the eggs.
Encourage unlimited eggs because dietary cholesterol never matters.

questions.correctAnswer: Consider eggs within the whole dietary pattern, especially the patient's LDL-C, saturated-fat intake and foods eaten with the eggs.
questions.explanation: Eggs contain cholesterol but relatively little saturated fat compared with foods such as bacon, butter or sausage often eaten alongside them. Context matters.
questions.clinicalPearl: Pattern-based counseling is more accurate than single-food moralizing.

questions.question: Which nutrients should a cardiovascular dietitian commonly compare across packaged foods?

options.text: Sodium, saturated fat, added sugar, trans-fat clues and fiber

questions.correctAnswer: Sodium, saturated fat, added sugar, trans-fat clues and fiber
questions.explanation: These label elements are directly useful for heart-healthy food selection.
questions.clinicalPearl: Per-serving values are meaningless unless the actual portion is also considered.

questions.question: If a nutrient provides 5% Daily Value or less per serving, it is generally considered:
questions.correctAnswer: Low
questions.explanation: The common Nutrition Facts rule of thumb is 5% DV or less is low and 20% DV or more is high.
questions.clinicalPearl: This heuristic is useful for sodium and saturated fat comparisons.

questions.question: Which change is most aligned with the 2026 AHA dietary guidance?

options.text: Increase sugary beverages while reducing water.
Choose minimally processed foods more often in place of ultraprocessed foods.
Replace vegetables with packaged snack foods.
Choose processed meat because it is high in protein.

questions.correctAnswer: Choose minimally processed foods more often in place of ultraprocessed foods.
questions.explanation: The 2026 AHA guidance explicitly favors minimally processed over ultraprocessed foods within the heart-healthy pattern.
questions.clinicalPearl: Processing level is not the only criterion, but it often clusters with sodium, refined starch, added sugar and unhealthy fat.

questions.question: What is the most appropriate cardiovascular advice for a person who does not drink alcohol?

options.text: Do not start drinking for presumed heart benefit.
Drink only on an empty stomach.
Start spirits because they contain no fat.
Start red wine daily for cardioprotection.

questions.correctAnswer: Do not start drinking for presumed heart benefit.
questions.explanation: Current AHA guidance does not recommend initiating alcohol for cardiovascular benefit.
questions.clinicalPearl: Observational associations are not a reason to prescribe alcohol.

questions.question: For a patient with obesity, high triglycerides and hypertension, which beverage change has the broadest cardiometabolic benefit?

options.text: Replace sugar-sweetened beverages with water or unsweetened beverages.
Add sugar to tea for energy.
Use regular soda but only with meals.

questions.correctAnswer: Replace sugar-sweetened beverages with water or unsweetened beverages.
questions.explanation: Reducing sugar-sweetened beverages lowers added sugar and energy intake and may help weight and triglyceride management.
questions.clinicalPearl: Beverage calories are often an efficient first target.

questions.question: Which fat is a defining primary fat source in a Mediterranean-style diet?
questions.correctAnswer: Olive oil
questions.explanation: Mediterranean-style eating uses olive oil as a central fat source.
questions.clinicalPearl: The pattern matters more than adding olive oil to an otherwise poor diet.

questions.question: Which protein pattern best fits Mediterranean-style eating?

options.text: Frequent legumes and fish, with poultry more often than red/processed meat

questions.correctAnswer: Frequent legumes and fish, with poultry more often than red/processed meat
questions.explanation: Mediterranean patterns emphasize plant foods, fish/seafood and lower amounts of red and processed meat.
questions.clinicalPearl: Protein source quality is a major cardiovascular lever.

questions.question: Which dessert is most characteristic of a Mediterranean-style pattern?
questions.correctAnswer: Fresh fruit
questions.explanation: Fruit is commonly used as dessert in Mediterranean-style eating, reducing added sugar and refined-food exposure.
questions.clinicalPearl: A healthy pattern can satisfy sweetness without making added sugar the default.

questions.question: Which grain choice best fits both Mediterranean and AHA heart-healthy guidance?

options.text: Barley or other intact whole grain

questions.correctAnswer: Barley or other intact whole grain
questions.explanation: Whole grains are a core feature of heart-healthy dietary patterns.
questions.clinicalPearl: Whole-grain quality can be assessed by ingredient list and fiber content.

questions.question: For a patient who needs a heart-healthy snack and has no nut allergy, which is most appropriate?

options.text: A small portion of unsalted nuts

questions.correctAnswer: A small portion of unsalted nuts
questions.explanation: Nuts supply unsaturated fats, fiber and plant protein; unsalted versions avoid extra sodium.
questions.clinicalPearl: Portion awareness matters because nuts are energy-dense.

questions.question: Wine is sometimes associated with Mediterranean eating. How should a dietitian counsel a non-drinker?

options.text: Do not recommend starting alcohol; the dietary pattern can be followed without wine.
Wine is mandatory for cardiovascular benefit.
Recommend two glasses with every meal.

questions.correctAnswer: Do not recommend starting alcohol; the dietary pattern can be followed without wine.
questions.explanation: Current AHA guidance is clear that people who do not drink should not start for heart health.
questions.clinicalPearl: Mediterranean diet ≠ alcohol prescription.

questions.question: What do DASH and Mediterranean-style diets strongly share?

options.text: Emphasis on vegetables, fruits, whole grains, legumes/nuts and healthier fat/protein sources

questions.correctAnswer: Emphasis on vegetables, fruits, whole grains, legumes/nuts and healthier fat/protein sources
questions.explanation: Both are plant-forward dietary patterns with strong overlap in foods associated with cardiovascular benefit.
questions.clinicalPearl: Teach common principles first, then the distinctive features of each pattern.

questions.question: A South Asian patient dislikes olives and asks whether a Mediterranean-style pattern is impossible. What is the best response?

options.text: Yes, the diet cannot be adapted culturally.
Yes, olives are mandatory at every meal.
No. The principles can be translated using culturally familiar vegetables, legumes, whole grains, nuts, fish and unsaturated plant oils.
Yes, only foods from Mediterranean countries count.

questions.correctAnswer: No. The principles can be translated using culturally familiar vegetables, legumes, whole grains, nuts, fish and unsaturated plant oils.
questions.explanation: Heart-healthy dietary patterns should be flexible enough to accommodate cultural and religious preferences.
questions.clinicalPearl: Mastery means understanding the pattern's principles, not copying a cuisine literally.

questions.question: Which substitution best fits a Mediterranean-style cardioprotective pattern?

options.text: Replace some processed meat meals with lentils or beans.

questions.correctAnswer: Replace some processed meat meals with lentils or beans.
questions.explanation: Legumes can displace processed meat while adding fiber and plant protein.
questions.clinicalPearl: Substitution questions are more clinically meaningful than isolated 'good food/bad food' questions.

questions.question: Which patient is following the Mediterranean pattern most faithfully?

options.text: One who adds olive oil to a diet dominated by processed meat and sweets.
One who drinks wine daily but rarely eats vegetables.
One whose overall diet is rich in plants, whole grains, legumes, nuts, fish and olive oil with limited highly processed foods.
One who eats only pasta and cheese.

questions.correctAnswer: One whose overall diet is rich in plants, whole grains, legumes, nuts, fish and olive oil with limited highly processed foods.
questions.explanation: Mediterranean eating is an overall dietary pattern, not a single food, oil or beverage.
questions.clinicalPearl: Avoid reducing evidence-based dietary patterns to one 'hero' ingredient.

questions.question: Which lipoprotein is a primary causal target in atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease prevention?

options.text: LDL-C and other apoB-containing atherogenic lipoproteins

questions.correctAnswer: LDL-C and other apoB-containing atherogenic lipoproteins
questions.explanation: Atherogenic apoB-containing particles, including LDL, drive atherosclerotic risk.
questions.clinicalPearl: Modern lipid management extends beyond total cholesterol.

questions.question: Under the 2026 ACC/AHA dyslipidemia guideline, what LDL-C goal is recommended for many very-high-risk secondary-prevention patients?
questions.correctAnswer: <55 mg/dL
questions.explanation: The 2026 guideline recommends an LDL-C goal below 55 mg/dL for secondary-prevention patients at very high risk.
questions.clinicalPearl: Know whether a number is a treatment goal, diagnostic threshold or risk-enhancing level.

questions.question: For very-high-risk secondary prevention, what non-HDL-C goal accompanies LDL-C <55 mg/dL in the 2026 guideline?
questions.correctAnswer: <85 mg/dL
questions.explanation: The 2026 guideline pairs LDL-C <55 mg/dL with non-HDL-C <85 mg/dL in very-high-risk secondary prevention.
questions.clinicalPearl: Non-HDL-C captures cholesterol in all atherogenic apoB-containing particles.

questions.question: How often should lipoprotein(a), Lp(a), generally be measured in adults according to the 2026 dyslipidemia guideline?

options.text: At least once in a lifetime

questions.correctAnswer: At least once in a lifetime
questions.explanation: The 2026 guideline recommends at least one lifetime Lp(a) measurement in adults.
questions.clinicalPearl: Lp(a) is largely genetically determined and is not meaningfully lowered by routine diet changes.

questions.question: Why can ApoB be useful in selected patients?

options.text: It estimates the number of atherogenic lipoprotein particles.
It is a marker of hydration only.

questions.correctAnswer: It estimates the number of atherogenic lipoprotein particles.
questions.explanation: Each atherogenic particle generally carries one ApoB molecule, so ApoB can help quantify particle burden.
questions.clinicalPearl: ApoB can add information when LDL-C and particle number are discordant, such as in hypertriglyceridemia.

questions.question: Which dietary issue should be assessed early in a patient with high triglycerides?

options.text: Excess energy, added sugars/refined carbohydrate and alcohol intake

questions.correctAnswer: Excess energy, added sugars/refined carbohydrate and alcohol intake
questions.explanation: High triglycerides can be driven by excess energy intake, alcohol, added sugars/refined carbohydrates, obesity and poorly controlled diabetes, among other causes.
questions.clinicalPearl: Always assess secondary causes, medications and glycemic control—not diet alone.

questions.question: At what triglyceride level does pancreatitis prevention become an especially urgent treatment consideration in the 2026 guideline?
questions.explanation: Triglycerides at or above 1,000 mg/dL are associated with particularly high pancreatitis risk and may require triglyceride-lowering therapy in addition to lifestyle treatment.
questions.clinicalPearl: Extremely high triglycerides change the immediate nutrition priority.

questions.question: Which dietary change is most likely to help lower LDL-C?

options.text: Replace butter and fatty processed meat with unsaturated plant fats and high-fiber plant foods.
Add coconut oil to each meal.

questions.correctAnswer: Replace butter and fatty processed meat with unsaturated plant fats and high-fiber plant foods.
questions.explanation: Reducing saturated/trans fat and increasing unsaturated fat and fiber is consistent with LDL-lowering dietary therapy.
questions.clinicalPearl: For LDL-C, saturated-fat replacement and soluble fiber are high-yield interventions.

questions.question: A patient with ASCVD says, 'If I eat perfectly, I can stop my statin.' What is the best dietitian response?

options.text: Diet is foundational but should complement—not independently replace—prescribed guideline-directed lipid-lowering therapy.
Use a supplement instead of medication.
Diet has no role once medication starts.
Stop the statin immediately if saturated fat is low.

questions.correctAnswer: Diet is foundational but should complement—not independently replace—prescribed guideline-directed lipid-lowering therapy.
questions.explanation: Nutrition and pharmacotherapy are complementary. Medication decisions belong with the prescribing clinician and should not be unilaterally changed.
questions.clinicalPearl: Never frame diet as a substitute for evidence-based secondary-prevention therapy.

questions.question: What does the 2026 dyslipidemia guideline say about dietary supplements for cholesterol management?

options.text: They are first-line for all patients.
They should replace statins after MI.
They are not recommended as a replacement for evidence-based lipid-lowering management.
They are always safer and more effective than medications.

questions.correctAnswer: They are not recommended as a replacement for evidence-based lipid-lowering management.
questions.explanation: The guideline emphasizes proven lifestyle and pharmacologic therapies rather than supplements for lipid lowering.
questions.clinicalPearl: Ask specifically about supplements because patients may omit them from medication histories.

questions.question: Which risk calculator replaced the older Pooled Cohort Equations in the 2026 ACC/AHA dyslipidemia guideline for many primary-prevention adults?
questions.correctAnswer: PREVENT-ASCVD
questions.explanation: The 2026 guideline uses the AHA PREVENT equations for contemporary 10- and 30-year ASCVD risk estimation.
questions.clinicalPearl: A dietitian need not prescribe statins, but should understand the risk framework guiding the medical plan.

questions.question: Which nutrition strategy best matches the lipid abnormality?

options.text: High LDL-C: prioritize saturated-fat replacement and soluble fiber; high triglycerides: also scrutinize alcohol, added sugars, refined carbohydrate and excess energy.
Use the same single-food prescription for every lipid disorder.
High LDL-C: increase butter; high triglycerides: increase sugary drinks.
High triglycerides: ignore weight and glycemic control.

questions.correctAnswer: High LDL-C: prioritize saturated-fat replacement and soluble fiber; high triglycerides: also scrutinize alcohol, added sugars, refined carbohydrate and excess energy.
questions.explanation: Different lipid phenotypes demand different nutrition priorities even within the same heart-healthy pattern.
questions.clinicalPearl: Mastery means matching intervention to phenotype.

questions.question: For many adults with excess weight, what initial weight-loss range can produce meaningful cardiometabolic benefit?

options.text: Weight loss has no effect on cardiometabolic risk

questions.correctAnswer: About 5–10% of starting body weight
questions.explanation: Even modest weight loss of about 5–10% can improve blood pressure, lipids and glycemic risk factors.
questions.clinicalPearl: Set clinically meaningful, achievable first targets.

questions.question: A patient weighs 92 kg. What is a 5% initial weight-loss target?
questions.correctAnswer: 4.6 kg
questions.clinicalPearl: Dietitians should calculate 5% and 10% targets instantly.

questions.question: A patient weighs 110 kg. What is a 10% weight-loss target?
questions.correctAnswer: 11 kg
questions.clinicalPearl: Translate percentages into concrete kilograms for counseling.

questions.question: What is required for sustained loss of body fat?

options.text: A sustained negative energy balance over time
Eliminating all dietary fat regardless of calories

questions.correctAnswer: A sustained negative energy balance over time
questions.explanation: Body-fat loss requires energy expenditure to exceed energy intake over time.
questions.clinicalPearl: Diet quality matters for health and adherence, but energy balance remains fundamental for weight change.

questions.question: Which approach best combines cardiovascular risk reduction with weight loss?

options.text: Use unlimited healthy oils because they are unsaturated.
Create an individualized energy deficit using a heart-healthy dietary pattern that is sustainable.
Use an extreme crash diet regardless of nutrient adequacy.
Focus only on scale weight and ignore blood pressure/lipids.

questions.correctAnswer: Create an individualized energy deficit using a heart-healthy dietary pattern that is sustainable.
questions.explanation: Sustainable energy reduction should preserve diet quality, protein adequacy and micronutrient intake.
questions.clinicalPearl: Weight loss is a tool, not the only outcome; monitor BP, lipids, glycemia and function.

questions.question: For an adult with hypertension and obesity, which statement is most accurate?

options.text: Blood pressure improves only after 30% weight loss.
Even about 5% weight loss can support blood-pressure improvement.
Weight has no relationship with blood pressure.

questions.correctAnswer: Even about 5% weight loss can support blood-pressure improvement.
questions.explanation: The 2025 hypertension guideline emphasizes weight management alongside DASH, sodium reduction, physical activity and alcohol reduction.
questions.clinicalPearl: Avoid single-factor counseling in multifactorial disease.

questions.question: Which dietary pattern usually lowers energy density while improving cardiovascular quality?

options.text: More fried foods and sugary drinks
Large amounts of oil added to every dish
More vegetables, fruits, legumes and whole grains with controlled portions of energy-dense fats

questions.correctAnswer: More vegetables, fruits, legumes and whole grains with controlled portions of energy-dense fats
questions.explanation: Plant-rich foods increase fiber and volume while supporting a heart-healthy nutrient profile.
questions.clinicalPearl: Even healthy fats need portion control during weight loss.

questions.question: Which outcome set best reflects high-quality cardiovascular weight-management follow-up?

options.text: Daily body-fat percentage from a consumer scale only
Weight/waist plus BP, lipids, glycemia, diet adherence and functional status

questions.correctAnswer: Weight/waist plus BP, lipids, glycemia, diet adherence and functional status
questions.explanation: Cardiovascular risk reduction is multidimensional; body weight is only one marker.
questions.clinicalPearl: A patient can improve risk factors before reaching a 'normal' BMI.

questions.question: After an acute coronary syndrome, which service should eligible patients be referred to because it improves recovery and secondary prevention?
questions.correctAnswer: Cardiac rehabilitation
questions.explanation: The 2025 ACS guideline recommends referral to cardiac rehabilitation after discharge.
questions.clinicalPearl: Nutrition counseling is one component of comprehensive cardiac rehabilitation.

questions.question: What is the long-term nutrition priority after MI?

options.text: A sustainable heart-healthy dietary pattern that reduces recurrent ASCVD risk
A temporary liquid diet for life

questions.correctAnswer: A sustainable heart-healthy dietary pattern that reduces recurrent ASCVD risk
questions.explanation: Secondary prevention is built on the overall dietary pattern, weight, activity, smoking status and guideline-directed medical therapy.
questions.clinicalPearl: There is no unique 'post-MI diet' disconnected from evidence-based ASCVD prevention.

questions.question: A post-CABG patient has poor appetite and is meeting only 40% of estimated needs. What is the immediate nutrition priority?

options.text: Keep the patient NPO without indication.
Ignore intake because long-term saturated fat matters more.
Assess nutritional risk and improve energy/protein intake while maintaining appropriate cardiac diet quality.

questions.correctAnswer: Assess nutritional risk and improve energy/protein intake while maintaining appropriate cardiac diet quality.
questions.explanation: After major surgery, underfeeding and malnutrition increase risk; early nutrition support is indicated when adequate oral intake cannot be maintained.
questions.clinicalPearl: Acute recovery priorities can temporarily differ from outpatient weight-loss priorities.

questions.question: What is the modern general surgical-nutrition principle regarding postoperative oral intake when clinically appropriate?

options.text: Keep all major-surgery patients NPO for 7 days.
Re-establish oral feeding as early as possible rather than prolonging unnecessary fasting.
Use parenteral nutrition routinely even when the gut works.

questions.correctAnswer: Re-establish oral feeding as early as possible rather than prolonging unnecessary fasting.
questions.explanation: ESPEN surgical guidance favors early oral feeding and avoidance of unnecessary perioperative fasting.
questions.clinicalPearl: Apply this with the surgical team's orders and the patient's hemodynamic/GI status.

questions.question: Why is adequate protein important after CABG?

options.text: It replaces the need for cardiac rehabilitation.
It supports wound healing and preservation/recovery of lean tissue.

questions.correctAnswer: It supports wound healing and preservation/recovery of lean tissue.
questions.explanation: Major surgery increases recovery needs; adequate protein supports tissue repair and muscle maintenance.
questions.clinicalPearl: Do not let 'heart healthy' become inadvertently low-protein in a frail postoperative patient.

questions.question: Why should glucose control be considered in postoperative cardiac nutrition care?

options.text: Glucose has no relevance after surgery.
All carbohydrates must therefore be eliminated.
Hyperglycemia can complicate recovery, and metabolic control is part of perioperative care.

questions.correctAnswer: Hyperglycemia can complicate recovery, and metabolic control is part of perioperative care.
questions.explanation: Perioperative guidelines include metabolic control, including blood glucose, as part of recovery.
questions.clinicalPearl: The answer is not zero carbohydrate; it is appropriate carbohydrate quality, amount and medical glycemic management.

questions.question: Which post-MI lunch is most aligned with secondary-prevention nutrition?

options.text: Processed-meat sandwich with butter and chips
Lentil salad with vegetables, whole grain and olive-oil dressing

questions.correctAnswer: Lentil salad with vegetables, whole grain and olive-oil dressing
questions.explanation: The first meal is plant-forward, high in fiber and uses unsaturated fat instead of saturated/trans-fat sources.
questions.clinicalPearl: Secondary prevention should look like a high-quality dietary pattern meal after meal.

questions.question: Which is the best dietitian message after MI regarding diet and medication?

options.text: Supplements replace both diet and medication.
Diet, cardiac rehabilitation and prescribed medications work together; none should be stopped without the treating clinician.

questions.correctAnswer: Diet, cardiac rehabilitation and prescribed medications work together; none should be stopped without the treating clinician.
questions.explanation: Secondary prevention is multidisciplinary and combines lifestyle with evidence-based pharmacotherapy.
questions.clinicalPearl: Dietitians should reinforce adherence and flag interactions without independently discontinuing drugs.

questions.question: A nutritionally depleted patient is 5 days post-CABG and overweight by BMI. What is the best priority?

options.text: Create a large calorie deficit immediately because BMI is high.
First restore adequate intake and support recovery; pursue intentional weight loss later when clinically stable.
Use only clear liquids for several weeks.

questions.correctAnswer: First restore adequate intake and support recovery; pursue intentional weight loss later when clinically stable.
questions.explanation: Postoperative healing and nutrition adequacy take priority when intake is poor or nutritional risk is present.
questions.clinicalPearl: BMI alone does not tell you whether aggressive calorie restriction is appropriate during acute recovery.

questions.question: Before discharge after CABG, which nutrition education is most useful?

options.text: A concrete plan for heart-healthy meals, sodium/fat label reading, adequate recovery nutrition and follow-up in cardiac rehabilitation.
A list of foods labeled simply 'good' or 'bad' with no context.
Advice to avoid all dietary fat.

questions.correctAnswer: A concrete plan for heart-healthy meals, sodium/fat label reading, adequate recovery nutrition and follow-up in cardiac rehabilitation.
questions.explanation: Discharge education should translate guidelines into shopping, meal planning, portions and follow-up.
questions.clinicalPearl: Knowledge without implementation planning rarely changes outcomes.

questions.question: What does sodium restriction primarily aim to reduce in heart failure?

options.text: Sodium-driven fluid retention and congestive symptoms

questions.correctAnswer: Sodium-driven fluid retention and congestive symptoms
questions.explanation: Excess sodium can promote fluid retention, worsening congestion in susceptible patients.
questions.clinicalPearl: Sodium restriction and fluid restriction are different interventions.

questions.question: What does a fluid restriction limit?

options.text: The total volume of fluids consumed, not just sodium intake

questions.correctAnswer: The total volume of fluids consumed, not just sodium intake
questions.explanation: Fluid restriction sets a volume limit across drinks and other countable fluids.
questions.clinicalPearl: A patient can follow a low-sodium diet yet exceed a fluid limit, or vice versa.

questions.question: Which example best illustrates sodium restriction without fluid restriction?

options.text: Choosing low-sodium foods while drinking fluids according to thirst/medical guidance with no prescribed volume cap.
Limiting all beverages to 1.5 L regardless of sodium.
Avoiding all water but eating salty processed food.

questions.correctAnswer: Choosing low-sodium foods while drinking fluids according to thirst/medical guidance with no prescribed volume cap.
questions.explanation: Sodium restriction targets sodium intake; fluid restriction targets total fluid volume.
questions.clinicalPearl: Quiz these concepts with scenarios, not definitions alone.

questions.question: Which example best illustrates fluid restriction?

options.text: Choosing unsalted nuts instead of salted nuts.
Keeping total daily countable fluids within a prescribed volume such as 1.5 L when ordered.

questions.correctAnswer: Keeping total daily countable fluids within a prescribed volume such as 1.5 L when ordered.
questions.explanation: A fluid restriction is a volume prescription and may include water, tea, coffee, milk, soup, ice and other fluids depending on local policy.
questions.clinicalPearl: Teach exactly what counts as fluid in the institution's protocol.

questions.question: According to the 2022 AHA/ACC/HFSA guideline, what is true about fluid restriction in advanced HF with hyponatremia?

options.text: It is strongly required for every patient with HF.
Its benefit for reducing congestive symptoms is uncertain.
It is contraindicated in every patient with HF.

questions.correctAnswer: Its benefit for reducing congestive symptoms is uncertain.
questions.explanation: The guideline rates the benefit of fluid restriction in advanced HF with hyponatremia as uncertain, underscoring the need for individualized medical guidance.
questions.clinicalPearl: Do not teach 'all HF patients need 1.5 L/day' as a universal rule.

questions.question: Why is daily body weight useful in heart failure self-monitoring?

options.text: Rapid changes can signal changing fluid status.

questions.correctAnswer: Rapid changes can signal changing fluid status.
questions.explanation: Rapid weight gain can reflect fluid accumulation and should be interpreted with symptoms and the care plan.
questions.clinicalPearl: Daily weights are about trend recognition, not body-fat change over 24 hours.

questions.question: Which product is the better choice for a patient with HF who has been told to reduce sodium, assuming other nutrients are similar?

options.text: A soup with 140 mg sodium per serving
A soup with 780 mg sodium per serving
A cured meat with 900 mg sodium per serving
A snack with 650 mg sodium per serving

questions.correctAnswer: A soup with 140 mg sodium per serving
questions.explanation: Lower-sodium choices reduce cumulative sodium burden and may help manage congestion.
questions.clinicalPearl: Check serving size: eating several servings changes the sodium total.

questions.question: A patient on a prescribed fluid restriction complains of thirst. Which strategy can help without silently exceeding the fluid allowance?

options.text: Drink several liters of water at once.
Eat more salty foods to stimulate thirst.
Spread allowed fluids across the day and use mouth care, ice chips if counted appropriately, and low-sodium foods to reduce thirst burden.

questions.correctAnswer: Spread allowed fluids across the day and use mouth care, ice chips if counted appropriately, and low-sodium foods to reduce thirst burden.
questions.explanation: Fluid-management strategies should improve comfort while respecting the prescribed plan; high sodium can worsen thirst and fluid retention.
questions.clinicalPearl: Local policies differ on how ice, gelatin and soup count toward fluid totals.

questions.question: Why is hyponatremia in heart failure not simply treated by telling every patient to eat more salt?

options.text: Because dietary salt cannot affect thirst.
It can reflect complex water and neurohormonal imbalance; management depends on volume status, medications and the medical plan.
Because all hyponatremia is caused by low protein.
Because sodium has no role in extracellular fluid.

questions.correctAnswer: It can reflect complex water and neurohormonal imbalance; management depends on volume status, medications and the medical plan.
questions.explanation: HF-associated hyponatremia is often dilutional and requires clinical assessment rather than reflex salt loading.
questions.clinicalPearl: Lab numbers must be interpreted in disease context.

questions.question: A patient with advanced HF has poor appetite, edema and unintentional weight loss. What should the dietitian do?

options.text: Restrict calories aggressively because edema increases body weight.
Ignore protein intake until edema resolves.
Assume weight is stable because scale weight has not fallen.
Assess for malnutrition and muscle loss while interpreting body weight cautiously because edema can mask tissue loss.

questions.correctAnswer: Assess for malnutrition and muscle loss while interpreting body weight cautiously because edema can mask tissue loss.
questions.explanation: Fluid accumulation can conceal loss of lean and fat mass; nutrition assessment should include intake history and physical findings.
questions.clinicalPearl: Dry weight and nutrition-focused assessment are crucial in congested patients.

questions.question: Which meal is most appropriate for many stable HF patients advised to avoid excessive sodium?

options.text: Instant noodles with seasoning packet and pickle
Freshly cooked dal with controlled salt, vegetables and whole grain, with sodium-rich condiments minimized.

questions.correctAnswer: Freshly cooked dal with controlled salt, vegetables and whole grain, with sodium-rich condiments minimized.
questions.explanation: Home-prepared minimally processed foods make sodium easier to control than many instant, cured and restaurant foods.
questions.clinicalPearl: Indian dietary counseling should quantify salt, pickles, papad, chutneys, packaged snacks and restaurant gravies.

questions.question: A patient with HFrEF, edema, CKD and potassium 5.6 mmol/L asks to use potassium chloride salt substitute to lower sodium. What is the safest response?

options.text: Ignore the potassium result because only sodium matters in HF.
Do not recommend it without medical review because hyperkalemia and CKD make added potassium potentially dangerous.

questions.correctAnswer: Do not recommend it without medical review because hyperkalemia and CKD make added potassium potentially dangerous.
questions.explanation: Potassium-based salt substitutes can reduce sodium intake but may be dangerous when potassium excretion is impaired or serum potassium is elevated.
questions.clinicalPearl: The best cardiovascular advice may change when renal and electrolyte constraints are present.
